curated_comment: FLAGGED: Value 1 cannot be confirmed from cited source (Ribeiro 2012:257). Page 257 discusses nominalized complements where possessive prefixes (wa- 1sg, a- 2sg, i- 3sg) mark the absolutive argument of deverbal nouns (e.g., wa-rira "my walking", kOÎUd̈̈) b́́)d́́) "turtle catching"), not overt absolutive case markers on independent NPs. Ribeiro (2012:54) explicitly classifies Karajá as nominative-accusative (backgrounding antipassive in an NOM-ACC language, not an ergative one). Ribeiro (2012:174) states: "Person agreement displays a strictly nominative pattern." The forms "S: -wa P: -bə̃" do not correspond to case markers in the grammar. Recommend expert review of original annotation. Value kept as 1 pending review.

Original value "?" resolved to 0. Free pronouns (dIkará̩ "I", kai "you", Ʌ́kɪ "s/he") are the same for S (intransitive subject) and A (transitive subject) — nominative pattern. Pronominal objects are obligatorily incorporated into the verb, not free pronouns with case marking. No ergative-absolutive distinction exists on 1st person pronouns. Source: Ribeiro 2012:174 (nominative agreement), 191-192 (pronominal objects incorporated).

Original value "?" resolved to 0. Full NPs show no overt case marking. Ribeiro (2012:51) explicitly states: "when both subject and object are nouns, they can only be distinguished by the word order, canonically SOV." Example: ha̩bu ha̩lOkOE 3-CTFG-TRANS-kill-PERF "The man killed the jaguar" — both NPs are zero-marked, distinguished only by position. Source: Ribeiro 2012:51.
